reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirty-five home runs projected at 22 years old, and the Statcast profile backs the shape of it: a 13.1% barrel rate and .480 xSLG say the power isn't a contact-driven mirage. The xwOBA sits at .350, which is meaningfully above a league-average hitter, and the gap between that and his .257 xBA tells you the value lives in the slug, not the hit tool. His chase and whiff rates are mid-range, nothing alarming, but the profile hinges on whether he can maintain contact quality against pitchers who've had a full look at him, because the hard-hit rate at 39.4% is below average despite the elite barrel numbers, suggesting the damage is concentrated rather than widespread. If that barrel efficiency holds, he's an everyday corner bat with genuine middle-of-the-order production; if pitchers find a way to shrink the damage zone, what's left is a slower-than-average defender at first or third hitting for modest average with walks that barely clear league rate.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .399 xwOBA at the plate and a 2.72 xERA on the mound aren't two players — they're the same guy, and both numbers sit at the 95th percentile or better against their respective populations. The contact profile has a wrinkle: a 31.5% whiff rate keeps the strikeout number elevated at 24.2%, but a 15.8% barrel rate and 93.2 mph average exit velocity mean the damage when he connects is severe enough that pitchers have no clean way out. On the mound, a 30.4% whiff rate and a 3.8% barrel rate allowed describe a starter who misses bats and suppresses hard contact without needing elite command to do it. The projection's .906 OPS and 35 home runs are what you get when both sides of the profile hold, and right now both sides are holding.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The bat-to-ball contact quality and the legs are both legitimate, but the plate discipline is the thing holding this profile back from a higher ceiling. His xSLG sits at .478 with a 91.2 mph average exit velocity, yet a 37.1% chase rate drags the actual production well below what the contact quality deserves, which is exactly why the projection lands at .293 OBP despite the 25 projected home runs. He's fast enough to steal 27 bases in a full season, and the 47.9% hard-hit rate means the power isn't a function of luck. If the chase rate ever tightens, the underlying contact profile upgrades him into a genuine middle-of-the-order piece; if it stays where it is, he's a productive, slightly frustrating outfielder who leaves value on the table every year.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the headline: 15% strikeouts across AAA & A+ & A translates to 18.7% at the MLB level, well below where most big-league hitters land, and that's with a .237 ISO in tow. At 21, Walker Jenkins is posting a .417 OBP across those three levels while walking 43 times against only 50 strikeouts in 324 plate appearances, a combination that scouts get excited about precisely because disciplined hitters with real power don't usually need much fixing. The ISO translates to .171 at the MLB equivalent, above what most regulars produce, so the power isn't a minor-league mirage, but his ceiling as an everyday center fielder depends on how much of that contact quality survives a full diet of big-league velocity. If it doesn't hold, you're looking at a useful bench piece; if it does, the Twins have a true regular.

reports.name: Gunnar Henderson

His 42.8% hard-hit rate is legitimately above average, but it's not translating into barrels, and a 6.9% barrel rate explains most of the gap between the contact quality you'd hope for and the .389 xSLG he actually earns. The projection spells it out plainly: 25 home runs across 722 plate appearances with a .223 average and a .707 OPS, which is a second-division regular's offensive line propped up by a position where the glove carries real weight. If the barrel rate climbs and the hard contact starts finding better angles, the offensive floor rises; if it doesn't, this is a plus defender who hits like one.

reports.name: Liam Doyle
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate jumps off the page, 11.5 K/9 at AA translating to 9.1 at the MLB level, but the walk rate is where this profile gets complicated. Fifty-two free passes in 98 innings at AA produces a BB/9 of 4.8, and the translation barely moves it, landing at 4.6 while the MLB average sits at 3.2. The K-BB% translates to 13.0 at the major-league level, right where the average falls, which is the quiet problem: elite strikeout stuff is being neutralized by the control, and nothing in this profile suggests the walks are an aberration rather than the shape of the pitcher. If the command sharpens, you have a rotation piece; if it doesn't, this is a depth arm cycling through the upper minors.

reports.name: Hunter Goodman
reports.published_report: Forty-one projected home runs from a catcher is a number that demands explanation, and the Statcast profile supplies one: a 15.5% barrel rate that ranks in the 95th percentile alongside a 90.3 mph average exit velocity. The problem is that the contact profile underneath the power is genuinely alarming, with a 32.6% strikeout rate and a 40.2% chase rate both landing near the bottom of the league, and the .227 xBA reflecting what happens when you put the ball in play that infrequently and that recklessly. The projection (.842 OPS, .528 SLG across 581 PA) is essentially a bet that the barrel rate is load-bearing enough to survive the strikeout volume, which it might be if pitchers keep attacking him in the zone. The moment they don't, the .314 OBP has nowhere to hide.

reports.name: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
reports.published_report: The 44 projected steals tell you what kind of player he is before you look at anything else. Chisholm's Statcast profile is a study in contradictions: 90.5 mph average exit velocity and a 10.4% walk rate sitting alongside a 30.9% whiff rate that pushes his xBA to .218, which is why the projection lands at .232 AVG and a .718 OPS despite genuine speed and enough contact quality to do damage when he connects. The contact rate is the hinge — if he can't cut into that whiff number, the power (.406 projected SLG) and speed play down because he's too often not putting the ball in play at all. What's left if it doesn't improve is a high-variance, high-entertainment second-division regular whose counting stats flatter the underlying offensive profile.

reports.name: Isaac Paredes
reports.published_report: The contact profile is legitimate and the power profile is not. The problem is that the exit velocity and hard-hit rate sit at the bottom of the league, 86.0 mph average exit velo and a 28.0% hard-hit rate, which makes the 21 projected home runs feel like they're borrowing against a pull-heavy approach that could regress further in a new park. reports.name: Yoshinobu Yamamoto
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.03 and the WHIP projection is 0.93, and those two numbers together describe a pitcher who doesn't beat himself. Yamamoto's Statcast profile is built on suppression rather than dominance: a 6.0% walk rate that ranks comfortably in the 88th percentile, contact that barely carries when it's made, and a chase rate of 32.9% that keeps hitters honest without requiring elite swing-and-miss numbers. The strikeout rate at 25.4% is fine, not fearsome, which means the profile hinges on that contact management holding, because if opponents start squaring him up more consistently the margin between a 3.03 xERA and an ordinary one gets thin fast. When it holds, 186 projected innings at a 2.75 ERA makes him one of the two or three most valuable arms in fantasy regardless of format.

reports.name: Michael Busch

reports.name: Logan Gilbert
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a little counterintuitive, and that tension is what Gilbert actually is. His strikeout rate sits at 26.6% and his walk rate at 6.4%, both well above league average, and he generates whiffs on nearly 29.7% of swings. But hitters who do make contact hit him hard, with a 10.3% barrel rate and 41.6% hard-hit rate that rank near the bottom of the league. He survives on process rather than soft contact: keep the ball off the barrel often enough, and a 3.73 xERA is the honest result. The projection, 186.1 innings, 3.71 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, is essentially his ceiling and his floor at the same time, a durable mid-rotation starter who wins with control and miss-bats and loses if his command wavers enough to let the hard contact he surrenders actually matter.

His 11.9% walk rate keeps the OBP livable at .353, and the 24 projected steals show enough speed to matter, just not to carry a fantasy profile the way it once did. Everything here hinges on whether the legs recover further: if sprint speed creeps back toward elite, the stolen base and gap-plus numbers look conservative, but if 27.1 ft/s is the new baseline, you're buying a high-OBP power hitter with modest speed, which is still a very good player, just a different one than Atlanta paid for.

He's chasing his way out of counts before walks become an option, which is why the .299 xwOBA lands 21st percentile even though his whiff rate (20.4%) is genuinely fine and his barrel and xBA metrics sit right at the middle of the pack. reports.name: Didier Fuentes
reports.published_report: A 31.8% strikeout rate with a 2.99 xERA is a young reliever who can genuinely miss bats, and the 97.2 mph fastball explains most of it. The whiff rate sits at 30.2% and the xwOBA against is .269, so the underlying quality is consistent across multiple angles. What the profile doesn't yet show is sharp command: the chase rate of 32.1% is ordinary, meaning he's earning those strikeouts mostly when hitters swing at his stuff in the zone rather than chasing off it, and if the 7.2% walk rate creeps up, that thin margin between dominant and hittable gets real thin. If the command holds, this profile translates to a legitimate high-leverage arm; without it, he's a hard-thrower who works around too much contact to trust in critical spots.

reports.name: Cole Carrigg
reports.published_report: Thirteen stolen bases projected across a part-time role at Coors tells you what kind of player this is before you read another number. Carrigg's 28.8 ft/s sprint speed lands him in the 86th percentile, and that engine animates a profile that otherwise sits right at league-average offense — .337 OBP, .784 OPS in 370 projected plate appearances. The fielding percentile (66th) says he's a functional outfielder, not a liability, which keeps the speed from being his only trick. If the hit tool holds at .266 and he gets regular at-bats in a park that tilts numbers upward, he's a useful second-division regular; if he can't handle better arms consistently, the speed and glove still carve out a legitimate bench role.

reports.name: Braylon Payne
reports.published_report: The ISO is the loudest thing in the profile: .265 across AA & A+, which translates to .173 at the MLB level, well clear of the .150 MLB average. At 19, that kind of raw power keeps you in the conversation regardless of what else is going on. What else is going on is a 29% strikeout rate across AA & A+ that translates to 31.5% against big-league pitching, and 48 walks across 447 plate appearances that level up to just 8.8% at MLB, barely a tick above the 8.5% MLB norm. The profile hinges on whether the contact rates tighten as he climbs, because if the strikeout translation holds in the majors, the power alone can't carry him, and what's left is an org-depth ceiling wrapped around a genuinely loud tool.

reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report: The contact-over-power bet is exactly what the Statcast card says it is: a 13.9% strikeout rate that almost nothing can touch, sitting against an average exit velocity of 83.5 mph that almost nothing can beat in the other direction. Durbin makes contact at an elite clip but doesn't do much with it, posting a .318 xSLG and a 2.8% barrel rate that together describe a hitter who survives by not missing rather than by punishing mistakes. The projection's 14 home runs and 19 stolen bases suggest the speed and volume fill in some of what the raw contact quality can't, but the whole profile hinges on whether a .249/.329/.383 line actually plays at third base every day or turns him into a useful bench piece who bats sixth when he starts. If the bat-to-ball skills age well and the defense holds at third, he's a second-division regular worth the roster spot; if pitchers ever start exploiting the swing more aggressively, the 83.5 mph exit velocity leaves him very little margin.

reports.name: Spencer Miles
reports.published_report: The xERA of 2.94 and xwOBA of .267 both sit at the 90th percentile, and the story behind both numbers is contact suppression, not strikeouts. Miles gets barrels at a 3.6% rate while his whiff rate of 18.5% is below average, meaning he limits damage through location and pitch shape rather than blowing hitters away. The 6.0% walk rate keeps him clean enough that the contact-management approach actually works, and a projected 1.06 WHIP over 94.2 innings suggests the underlying quality is already showing up in outcomes. If the barrel suppression regresses, the modest swing-and-miss gives him no fallback, but right now he profiles as a high-leverage reliever whose results are exactly as good as his contact profile says they should be.

A 32.3% whiff rate and a 31.7% strikeout rate, both in the bottom decile of the league, are doing so much damage to his average floor that a .214 xBA makes a .225 projection feel optimistic rather than conservative. The exit velocity is genuine: 91.5 mph average and a 12.3% barrel rate say the power is still there when he makes contact, and an xSLG of .396 confirms the shape of a 19-homer threat even in a degraded season. But a 7.4% walk rate can't compensate for that much swing-and-miss, and the .299 xwOBA is what you get when a hitter barrels the ball plenty and misses it far too often. He's a second-division regular right now, not a broken player, but the version that made him a cornerstone doesn't exist as long as the strikeout rate stays where it is.

reports.name: Riley Quick
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, the walk rate is the whole argument. Across AA & A+ & A, Quick has racked up 108 strikeouts in 77.6 innings, 12.5 per nine, but the 46 walks push his BB/9 to 5.3, and when you translate that to an MLB context the walks get worse: a 5.1 BB/9 where the average starter gives up 3.2. The K-BB% sits at 19% across those levels, which grades well in the minor-league pool, but the MLB-equivalent strips it to 12.5%, just under the 13.5% MLB mean. The whole profile hinges on whether he can tighten the zone enough to stop giving away free baserunners, because the strikeout stuff will play up; if the command stays where it is, the ceiling and floor land in the same place, depth arm.

reports.name: Manuel Pena
reports.published_report: The bat is loud and the profile is narrow. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Manuel Peña is hitting .305/.345/.555 with 31 home runs in 506 plate appearances, and his .251 ISO ranks at the 93rd percentile in the hitter pool. The translation to MLB dims it some: that power likely plays to a .181 ISO, but his 6.4% translated walk rate is thin for a first baseman who strikes out at a 25.1% translated clip, and there is not enough patience in the profile to cushion contact variance. This profile hinges entirely on whether a left-handed first baseman can sustain enough contact quality against major-league arms to stay useful, and if the contact holds he's a bench bat who can do real damage in the right matchup — if it doesn't, the on-base floor is too shallow for a regular role.

report_llm.text: The barrel rate is 12.3% — genuinely elite contact quality — and the chase rate of 22.2% puts him among the most disciplined zone-hunters in the game. But the strikeout rate sits at 31.6%, and that's the whole contradiction: he sees the zone well enough to walk at 10.5% yet still whiffs on a third of his swings, which drags his xBA to .211 and explains why the power doesn't fully show up in the slash line. The projection carries 25 home runs across 616 PA, which tracks given the barrel quality, but a .219 AVG and .310 OBP make him a below-average producer at a position that demands more. If the whiff rate ever comes down to match what his chase discipline says it should be, there's a real everyday first baseman here; if it doesn't, he's a low-OBP power source you roster for the home runs and tolerate everywhere else.

reports.name: Keider Montero
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument: 5.5% BB% sits at the 93rd percentile among starters, and when you pair that kind of command with a 3.42 xERA, you get a guy who limits damage without needing to miss bats. Because he doesn't miss many, a 16.6% K% and 18.3% Whiff% are both bottom-of-the-barrel figures, the profile lives and dies on whether hitters keep making weak enough contact to validate the xwOBA of .287. The contact quality numbers are middling enough (88.6 mph average exit velo, 7.0% Barrel%) to keep him functional, but if opponents start squaring him up more consistently, there's no swing-and-miss floor to fall back on. If the command holds and the soft contact continues, he's a legitimate mid-rotation piece in Detroit; if hitters adjust and start hunting in the zone, you're left with a back-end arm posting an ERA well north of that 3.63 projection.

reports.name: Chase Harlan
reports.published_report: The .403 OBP and 13% walk rate across A+ & A are the loud part of this profile. At 19, Chase Harlan is doing real plate discipline work, 51 walks in 396 PA, and the .298/.403/.509 line puts him at the 93rd percentile in OPS among this hitter pool. The translation is where it gets honest: his ISO drops from .211 to .137 MLB-equivalent, below league average, and his strikeout rate lands at 25.4% where the MLB average sits at 22.0, so the power that reads as a weapon at A-ball may arrive as fringe-average at the highest level. If the approach holds and the in-zone contact gains enough quality, he's a second-division regular at third; if the hit tool stalls and the strikeouts inflate further, what remains is a patient bench bat with a narrow role.

reports.name: Nathan Flewelling
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the most interesting thing in this profile, and it might also be the most misleading part. At A+ across 486 plate appearances, Flewelling has drawn 71 walks against 132 strikeouts, a 15% walk rate that translates to roughly 11% at the MLB level, a figure meaningfully ahead of where MLB hitters sit on average, but his 27% strikeout rate at A+ becomes something closer to 30.5% when you run it through the level adjustment, and that's a hard number to build a catcher's career around. The .208 ISO at A+ is loud for a 19-year-old at that level, yet it softens to about .144 in MLB-equivalent terms, which lands right at the league-average power band, meaning the profile that looks like a power-and-patience bat in High-A looks more like a fringe regular once you translate it. Everything here hinges on whether the strikeout rate bends as he climbs; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench catcher with acceptable plate discipline and middling pop.

reports.name: Brody Hopkins
reports.published_report: 120 strikeouts across 93 AAA innings is the loud number, and it earns him a look every time someone scans the organizational depth. The 92 walks in those same innings are why the look doesn't last long. The MLB-equivalent translation puts his BB/9 at 7.3 where the average pitcher sits at 3.2, and his K-BB% translates to 8.1 against a majority of pitchers clearing 13.5, so the strikeout ability isn't coming close to compensating for the command deficit. If the control ever tightens enough to stop turning counts into walks, there's a depth arm worth tracking; until then, the 1.7 WHIP and 5.2 ERA at AAA are the expected output from a pitcher giving away bases faster than he's recording outs.

reports.name: Ian Seymour
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the spine of this profile: 35.1% puts him in the 90th percentile, and he converts that into strikeouts at 28.8%, which is legitimately elite company. When hitters are chasing at that clip and whiffing on 29.2% of swings, the .295 xwOBA and 3.63 xERA start to make sense, even against a fastball sitting 91.4 mph that rates near the bottom of the league. That velocity floor is the thing — if hitters learn to lay off or simply punish a below-average heater without the element of surprise, the deception-dependent strikeout rate compresses and that 10.0% barrel rate becomes the number running the show instead of the chase rate. If the arsenal holds, he's a back-end starter who outperforms his stuff; if it doesn't, the 4.31 ERA projection looks closer to floor than ceiling.

reports.name: Bubba Chandler
reports.published_report: 98.4 mph on the fastball and a 5.7% barrel rate are the two things you circle, then you look at 11.6% walks and wonder how long Pittsburgh lets this play out. The stuff grades loud, with 95th-percentile velocity and spin that backs it up at 2402 rpm, but hitters aren't chasing at 28.6% and whiffing at only 22.5%, which means the heater isn't finishing them the way the raw numbers suggest it should. The xERA sits at 4.00, contact quality is manageable, and the projection lines up at 4.27 over 158.5 innings, so this isn't a disaster profile; it's a pitcher who can miss barrels without yet missing bats, and the whole thing hinges on whether the command tightens enough to make the walk rate something other than a drain on every start. Sixty-five walks against 77 strikeouts across 419 AA plate appearances is a real skill set, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his walk rate at 12.0%, nearly half again what a typical big-leaguer draws, but the ISO translates to .098 in that same context while most MLB hitters land around .150, which means the bat has to do everything through contact and speed. Fifty-eight stolen bases at AA will get scouts to the ballpark, but if the gap between his on-base ability and his slugging (.370 at AA, 36th percentile among this pool) doesn't close, he's a bench piece who lives on patience and legs rather than a regular. The ceiling is thin enough that this profile hinges entirely on whether that speed translates and the hit tool holds, and if contact regresses, the .395 OBP at AA becomes the whole argument.

reports.name: Jaison Chourio
reports.published_report: Forty stolen bases across AA & A+ at 21 years old is the loudest thing on this card, and the plate discipline surrounding it, 72 walks against 104 strikeouts, a 14% walk rate that translates to roughly 11.3% at the MLB level, suggests the speed isn't just a tool running ahead of the rest of the profile. The problem is the power, or the lack of it: a .137 ISO at these levels translates to .116 against big-league pitching, well short of the MLB average, and nothing here suggests that gap closes. If the bat-to-ball and zone judgment hold, he becomes a high-OBP, high-speed center fielder worth a bench spot or more; if the power ceiling is exactly what the translation says it is, what's left is a depth piece whose value lives entirely on his legs.

Across AAA & A+, Sandlin has issued 35 walks in 69.3 innings, and the translation puts his BB/9 at 4.2 against an MLB average of 3.2 — a gap that doesn't close on its own. reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing on this card, and it's also the problem. At A+ in 2026, Blake Mitchell has drawn 113 walks in 511 plate appearances, a 22% clip that sits at the 99th percentile of his pool, and he's added 27 stolen bases and 23 home runs on top of it, a legitimately unusual combination for a catcher at 21. But the .234 average against a .346 BABIP tells you the strikeouts aren't disappearing, and when that contact rate translates to an MLB-equivalent 36.8% K%, what survives the jump is a 15.4% walk rate propped up against average power at .152 ISO. The whole profile hinges on whether the discipline holds as pitchers locate better, because if the strikeouts climb and the walks compress even modestly, the .234 average becomes the story rather than the footnote. If it works, he's a patient, borderline-average offensive catcher who runs; if it doesn't, the bench is the ceiling.

The power doesn't travel: a .117 ISO at AA becomes .11 in an MLB context, and the average sits at .15. If the command tightens, there's a real arm here; if it doesn't, the 34 walks across 51.3 innings at AAA mark the ceiling.

reports.name: Juan Flores
reports.published_report: The power is loud enough to get your attention — .196 ISO across AA & A+, which translates to .143 at the MLB level, roughly what the average big-leaguer produces. But everything around it is a problem. A 26% strikeout rate at the minor-league level becomes 28.2% once you run it through an MLB lens, and the walk rate translates to 5.8% when MLB hitters are drawing walks at 8.5%. At 20 behind the dish, the developmental clock cuts him some slack, but the .295 OBP across 379 plate appearances is the honest weight of that profile: the bat-to-ball issues and the passivity are both real, and neither one can be papered over by the pop. If the feel for the zone improves as he matures, he might grow into a second-division catcher with interesting right-handed thump; if it doesn't, the floor here is a bench or organizational depth piece.

reports.name: Tate Kuehner
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here, and it doesn't go well. In 55 innings at AAA, Kuehner has issued 27 walks, and when that number translates, it lands at 4.0 BB/9 against a backdrop where big-league starters are running closer to 3.2 — a gap that doesn't close just by arriving. The strikeout rate translates to 8.2 per nine, just a tick below the MLB mean, so there's no miss rate carrying the control problem. At 25 with a K-BB% that would sit below average in the majors, the ceiling here is depth arm and the floor is the same place.
reports.report: The sample covers 55 IP in Triple-A, so confidence is moderate; there's no repeatable way to retire hitters in the line yet. The failure point is the strikeout-to-walk result, which does not support a firm starter projection. A rotation role is not supported by the current line; the floor is organizational depth or a low-leverage bullpen assignment.

reports.name: Dameivi Tineo
reports.published_report: 141 strikeouts across A+ & A in 94.4 innings is a number that commands attention, and the 13.5 K/9 sits at the 96th percentile of his pool. The problem is sitting right next to it: 66 walks, a BB/9 of 6.3 that translates to 6.4 in MLB-equivalent terms while the mlb_avg for that same translation is 3.2. The strikeout rate translates to nearly league-average MLB production, which means if the walks don't tighten, there's no margin left to work with. The whole profile lives or dies on whether he finds the zone enough to let the swing-and-miss matter — and right now the ceiling is a depth arm, not because the stuff says so, but because the command does.
reports.report: The walks are the separator, not the stuff. The swing-and-miss is real enough to keep a rotation path open. Starter upside is still alive, but the current command creates real bullpen risk. The sample covers 94.4 IP in High-A and Single-A, so confidence is low.

reports.name: Cooper Hjerpe
reports.published_report: Fifty-six strikeouts in 38 innings across three levels is the loud part of this profile, and it translates to a 9.7 K/9 at the big-league level — the swing-and-miss has teeth. The walk rate is the whole problem: 31 walks in those same 38 innings, translating to 5.3 per nine where MLB starters average 3.2, and a K-BB% that lands at 12.6% once you run it through the translation. If the command doesn't tighten, the strikeouts become a curiosity rather than a carrying tool, and what's left is a reliever who misses bats but can't hold the zone consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Jostin Florentino
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate stands out — 11.0 K/9 at A+, which translates to 8.3 at the MLB level, right at league average punch. But thirty-three free passes across 63 innings is the whole argument: the MLB-equivalent BB/9 comes out to 4.6, well above where big-league starters live, and that gap is the ceiling. The K-BB% grades at 72nd percentile among his pitcher pool, which tells you the stuff is doing real work, but the command needs to tighten substantially for him to be anything more than a depth arm. If it doesn't, that's exactly what he becomes.
